submission.natural_language_explanation: N944+ is a layer-0, context-free piece-identity ('unigram') detector, not a lookahead: its strength is a fixed lookup on the current GPT-NeoX piece alone, identical at every occurrence in any sentence and at any position (' Sign' 1.84 and 'Sign' 1.76 in every context, ' د' 1.23 in every Arabic context, 'edu' 1.26 inside 'Seduction'; replaying the cached scan reproduces the whole 50,304-piece table to 4 decimals; 100% of the input attribution sits on the peak token; position explains 2% of variance; zero-ablating the pole moves next-token probabilities only diffusely, KL 0.0025 with no concentrated target token set; the tokens after its peaks are unrelated: 's' after 'Sign', 'ction' after 'edu', 'مشق' after ' د'), so 'predicted active' means the current token is one of its firing pieces at or above the active line 0.25xmax = 0.44 - 2,409 of 50,304 pieces (2,191 Latin, 145 other-script alphabetic, 73 non-letter), graded with 1,738 pieces at or above 0.5, 1,007 at 0.6, 292 at 0.8 and 83 at 1.0 - strongest on ' Sign' 1.84 (the max), 'Sign' 1.76, 'Email' 1.60, ' cookies' 1.49, 'sign' 1.34, ' staying' 1.27, ' Here' 1.16 and 'Here' 1.22, ' sign' 1.12, ' please' 1.08, 'Write'/'Writing' 1.01/1.01, ' Follow' 1.02, ' Drive' 1.22, 'Leave' 1.20, 'Keep' 1.02, ' hidden' 0.95, ' lived' 1.09, ' live' 1.02, ' living' 0.64, ' signing' 0.89, 'Users' 0.91, ' Password' 0.50, 'Acknowledgments'/'Acknowledgements' 1.12/1.08, 'Affirmed'/'AFFIRMED' 1.15/1.11, 'html' 0.94, 'com' 0.99, ' alerts' 0.60, plus a graded 0.94-1.30 band of Latinate word stems (' nause' 1.25, ' aest' 1.27, ' Neut' 1.29, ' extrac' 1.19, ' immunos' 0.97, ' nucleic' 0.95, ' agarose' 0.97, ' antif' 1.04, ' clust' 0.95, ' custod' 0.95, ' grat' 0.96, ' salv' 0.95, ' colleg' 0.96, ' pyl' 1.05, ' frequ' 1.10, ' guid' 1.04, ' marg' 1.05, ' ger' 1.14, ' Libert' 1.20, ' lieu' 1.22, 'doibase' 1.30) and the non-Latin alphabetic pieces that carry most of its firing mass (' د' 1.23, ' ق' 0.91, 'ود' 0.89, 'ط' 0.87, ' ح' 0.82, ' ت' 0.81, ' ع' 0.70, 'ت' 0.63, Greek 'ίναι' 1.06, ' επι' 1.04, Cyrillic 'ут' 1.01, 'из' 0.94, CJK '지' 0.92, '么' 0.79; 28% of Arabic pieces, 14% Greek, 11% Cyrillic, 8% CJK against 5% of Latin and 1.4% of non-letters); it is piece-exact rather than semantic or morphological, so same-word or same-field neighbours that are different pieces stay below the line (' signal' -0.01, ' signals' 0.05, ' design' -0.07, ' significant' -0.03, ' there' -0.08, ' where' -0.17, ' Then' -0.11, ' cookie' 0.16, ' emails' 0.16, ' username' 0.01, ' login' -0.09, ' Users' -0.03, ' nausea' 0.11, ' aesthetic' -0.17, ' neutrophil' -0.13, ' extracellular' -0.07, ' lethal' 0.23, ' liver' -0.14, ' standing' 0.15, ' notice' 0.06, ' notifications' 0.21, ' alert' 0.05, ' subscribe' 0.29, ' people' -0.17, ' world' -0.01), and every function word, determiner, pronoun, digit and punctuation mark sits at the GELU floor (-0.01 to -0.17: ' the' -0.01, ' and' -0.01, ' of' 0.00, ',' -0.01, '.' 0.00), with the 13 pieces the scan used more than 1,000 times never firing at all; rival_explanations: It fires on a semantic 'notice and contact' field - signs, email, cookies, please, follow, alerts, notices - so an unseen text about warnings, subscriptions or contact details should fire even when it uses different words (' alert', ' notice', ' warning', ' subscribe', ' notifications').

It is a morphological word-family detector for the 'sign', 'live'/'lived', 'stay'/'staying' and 'write' stems, so any inflection or derivation of those stems should fire (' signals', ' signature', ' design', ' assigned', ' liver', ' alive'), not only the particular pieces seen.

top_examples.text:
Activation of the bone morphogenetic protein receptor by H11kinase/Hsp22 promotes cardiac cell growth and survival.
H11 kinase/Hsp22 (H11K) is a chaperone promoting cardiac cell growth and survival through the activation of Akt, a downstream effector of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K). In this study, we tested whether H11K-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway is mediated by the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling, both in a transgenic mouse model with cardiac-specific overexpression of H11K and in isolated cardiac myocytes. Microarrays in hearts from transgenic compared to wild-type mice showed an upregulation of the BMP receptors Alk3 and BMPR-II, and of their ligand BMP4 (P<0.01 versus wild type). Activation of the BMP pathway in transgenic mice was confirmed by increased phosphorylation of the "canonical" BMP effectors Smad 1/5/8 (P<0.01 versus wild type). In isolated myocytes, adenovirus-mediated overexpression of H11K was accompanied by a significant (P<0.01) increase in PI3K activity, phospho-Akt, Smad 1/5/8 phosphorylation and [(3)H]phenylalanine incorporation, and by a 70% reduction in H(2)O(2)-mediated apoptosis. All these effects were abolished by the BMP antagonist noggin. In presence of BMP4, Smad 1/5/8 phosphorylation was enhanced by 5-fold on H11K overexpression but decreased by 3-fold on H11K knockdown (P<0.01 versus control), showing that H11K potentiates the BMP signaling. In pull-down experiments, H11K increased both the association of Alk3 and BMPR-II together, and their interaction with the transforming growth factor-beta-activated kinase (TAK)1, a "noncanonical" mediator of the BMP receptor signaling. TAK1 inhibition prevented H11K-mediated activation of Akt. Therefore, potentiation of the BMP receptor by H11K promotes an activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway mediated by TAK1, which dictates the physiological effects of H11K on cardiac cell growth and survival.

This book bridges communication theory and practice to foreground an important message: positive communication matters. By examining closely how people talk to each other at home or at work, this book enables undergraduate and graduate students to communicate more positively. The Art of Positive Communication is an ideal text for undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in interpersonal communication courses and as a supplemental text to inspire all students to communicate better.

Who appoints EU Commissioners?
The Commissioners are proposed by the Council of the European Union, on the basis of suggestions made by the national governments, and then appointed by the European Council after the approval of the European Parliament.
Who is president von der Leyen?
|Ursula von der Leyen|
|Assumed office 1 December 2019|

Who is European Commission?
The Commission is composed of the College of Commissioners from 27 EU countries. Together, the 27 Members of the College are the Commission’s political leadership during a 5-year term.
How is European Commission President elected?
European Council proposes a candidate for the European Commission President, taking into account the elections to the European Parliament and after having held the appropriate consultations. Members of the European Council vote by qualified majority.
Why does the EU have two parliaments?
The EU’s national governments unanimously decided in 1992 to lay down in the EU treaty where the EU institutions are officially seated. Any change in the current system would need changing the treaty, which requires unanimity among all member states governments and ratification by each of their national parliaments.
Where is EU Parliament?
The European Parliament meets annually for about 12 one-week plenary sessions in Strasbourg, France. Most other work (e.g., committee meetings) takes place in Brussels.
Are EU members elected?
Until 2019, 751 MEPs were elected to the European Parliament, which has been directly elected since 1979. No other EU institution is directly elected, with the Council of the European Union and the European Council being only indirectly legitimated through national elections.
Who is the current UK EU commissioner?
Julian King (diplomat)
Can the European Parliament dismiss the commission?
The European Parliament has the right to approve and dismiss the European Commission. The candidate is elected by the EP. The EP can censure the Commission and ultimately dismiss it

A high quality science education not only provides the foundations for understanding the world around us, but equips pupils with essential knowledge and life skills needed in a changing world. At Minehead Middle School science is taught in attainment groups in years 7 and 8, and in mixed attaining classes in years 5 and 6.
The new National Curriculum is followed in all year groups with a bespoke themed approach in Key Stage 2. The Oxford University Press ‘Activate’ programme of study is then taught in Key Stage 3. This enables pupils to engage with up to date, relevant and interesting concepts thereby providing a solid foundation for further work in years 9, 10 and 11.
The science curriculum links closely with the maths and Design Technology curriculum, with pupils using practical investigations to reinforce key concepts in Biology, Chemistry and Physics.
In years 5 and 6 the teaching is done by the year teams, whereas in years 7 and 8 all the science is taught by experienced specialist teachers.

The League believes that global climate change is the most serious environmental challenge of our time and that aggressive action is needed if we are to avoid irrevocable damage to our planet. An advocate of strong U.S. action to reduce the threat of global warming since the 1990s, the League has made global climate change an action priority since 2006.
But it will take action from individuals and government at every level -- local, state, national, and international -- to avert dangerous climate change. And every League has an important role to play in this effort. By raising public awareness of the causes and likely impacts of climate change, by helping citizens learn what they can do to curb global warming, and by building broad support for effective climate solutions, local and state Leagues can help put our country -- and our planet -- on the path to a sustainable future.
Whether you focus on educating and empowering the members of your League or you broaden your outreach to other organizations in your community, there are many things your League can do to help build the momentum for climate solutions.
Climate change column in your Voter. Raise members' awareness of climate change and what they can do about it with a regular column in your Voter. Feature energy-saving tips, action alerts on climate and energy legislation, new findings from climate scientists, and information about "green" events in your community.
What climate impacts are projected for our community?
How can we prepare for these projected impacts?
What is my carbon footprint and what will I do to reduce it?
What energy savings programs do our utility companies offer?
Who is working on climate change in our community and what are they doing?
Informational meeting for your members. Present a program on climate change for your members. (Review Preparing for a Meeting on Climate Change in this toolkit for suggestions.) Be sure to include information about League positions and action on global climate change.
EcoTeam. Members of your League might be interested in supporting each other in going on a Low Carbon DIet: A 30-Day Program to Lose 5000 Pounds. An illustrated workbook is available to walk team members through a step-by-step process to dramatically reduce their carbon footprints.
Community forum. Sponsor -- or better still, co-sponsor -- a goal-oriented community meeting on climate change. Provide an opportunity for audience members to discuss solutions -- what they as individuals, and what all of you as a community, can do.
